269   1.3 Crop growth [SOURCE: Page_266]

270   The crop growth is calculated only in agricultural SUs at daily time steps based on the principles of the AqYield [SOURCE: Page_266]

271   crop model (Constantin et al., 2015). Crop growth, both aerial and root, controls crop transpiration and crop yield. [SOURCE: Page_266]

272   The crop aerial development is simulated using a crop coefficient representing foliar growth. Crop coefficient [SOURCE: Page_266]

273   dynamics are a function of crop transpiration, development stage (phenology), and various parameters specific to [SOURCE: Page_266]

274   a given species. Globally, the crop coefficient increases until the flowering stage and then declines until the [SOURCE: Page_266]

275   harvesting stage. Crop development stages, particularly the flowering and maturity stages, are simulated based [SOURCE: Page_266]

276   on the concept of growing degree days, with threshold values of the growing degree days and parameters [SOURCE: Page_266]

277   specific to each species and cultivar precocity class. [SOURCE: Page_266]

278   The actual crop transpiration is calculated with an empirical function of the maximum transpiration and soil water [SOURCE: Page_266]

279   available to roots. The maximum transpiration depends on the crop coefficient and ET$_0$ minus soil evaporation. [SOURCE: Page_266]

280   The soil water available to roots varies as a function of root growth. Root growth depends on the cumulative daily [SOURCE: Page_266]

281   effective temperature, a species root-growth coefficient and a reduction coefficient linked to the soil structure. [SOURCE: Page_266]

282   The crop yield is calculated at harvest as a function of the potential yield, locally defined for a species or cultivar [SOURCE: Page_266]

283   precocity class, and the water satisfaction index defined as the ratio of the actual crop transpiration to the [SOURCE: Page_266]

284   maximum crop transpiration during the cropping season. [SOURCE: Page_266]

285   1.4 Crop and agricultural withdrawal management [SOURCE: Page_266]

286   1.4.1 Crop management [SOURCE: Page_266]

287   The model simulates farmer management decisions at daily time steps and for every agricultural SU. The [SOURCE: Page_266]

288   decisions are related to several practices (tillage, sowing, harvesting and irrigation), but only one practice, [SOURCE: Page_266]

289   respecting a given priority order, is operated each day. Technical interventions are simulated over a given user- [SOURCE: Page_266]

290   defined period of the year. Within this window period, the exact dates of technical operations and amounts of [SOURCE: Page_266]

291   water applied to crops are determined according to decision rules based on crop growth and development [SOURCE: Page_266]

292   characteristics, soil type and water content, and weather conditions. These rules, the priority order between [SOURCE: Page_266]

293   practices, and the window period for each practice and crop may be adjusted to the context via a user-defined set [SOURCE: Page_266]

37   14 [SOURCE: Page_266]

38                                                                                                                      15 [SOURCE: Page_267]

294   of parameters. The thusly simulated technical operations modify the other model variables. Tillage operations [SOURCE: Page_267]

295   affect the soil structure and thus the soil water content capacity. The sowing and harvesting dates determine the [SOURCE: Page_267]

296   start and end, respectively, of crop cycles. Irrigation decisions trigger water withdrawal operations from REs or [SOURCE: Page_267]

297   RSs and influence the SU soil water content and thus the crop growth and crop yield. The irrigation demand by [SOURCE: Page_267]

298   the farmer depends on the crop water requirement according to its development stage but also accounts for [SOURCE: Page_267]

299   equipment constraints through a minimum delay between two irrigations. [SOURCE: Page_267]

300   Complementary to the presentation of Murgue et al. (2014), Appendix A details the simulation rules applied to [SOURCE: Page_267]

301   farmer management decisions. [SOURCE: Page_267]

302   1.4.2 Management of the withdrawal from water resources [SOURCE: Page_267]

303   Management of water withdrawal for irrigation purposes is modelled at a daily time step for each water resource [SOURCE: Page_267]

304   dedicated to irrigation, with RS being first withdrawn, then RE. This approach prioritizes stream water as a [SOURCE: Page_267]

305   resource used for irrigation. [SOURCE: Page_267]

306   The total irrigation water demand on a given resource (RE or RS) is determined as the sum of the daily farmer’s [SOURCE: Page_267]

307   irrigation demand for all irrigable agricultural SUs linked to that resource. If the available water in the resource is [SOURCE: Page_267]

308   larger than the total irrigation water demand, the water demand is satisfied by the water withdrawal, and the [SOURCE: Page_267]

309   irrigation volume provided to each SU is equal to its demand. Otherwise, the withdrawal volume corresponds to [SOURCE: Page_267]

310   the available water volume in the resource, and the irrigation volume applied to each SU is proportionally reduced [SOURCE: Page_267]

311   compared to the water demands. [SOURCE: Page_267]

324   1.5 Computer implementation [SOURCE: Page_268]

325   The MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs model was developed within the OpenFLUID platform (Fabre et al., 2020; Fabre [SOURCE: Page_268]

326   et al., 2010). This platform facilitates model building by sequentially coupling blocks of code, called simulators, [SOURCE: Page_268]

327   with each simulator supporting one of the main model functions. The OpenFLUID platform achieves the coupling [SOURCE: Page_268]

328   of models via the exchange of simulation variables varying both in space and time. The overall structure of the [SOURCE: Page_268]

329   spatial domain is managed using a graph where the nodes are the spatial units (here, SUs, RSs, GUs, and REs) [SOURCE: Page_268]

330   and the edges are these relations between the above spatial units (hydrological or agronomic links). MHYDAS- [SOURCE: Page_268]

331   Small-Reservoirs consists of 16 simulators described in Appendix B and considers a total of 40 variables. All [SOURCE: Page_268]

332   simulators were written in the C++ language, which allows unit-oriented data entry (Jordan, 1990). [SOURCE: Page_268]

333   1.6 Input and simulated variables, parameters and initial conditions [SOURCE: Page_268]

334   The input variables are weather variables, namely, rainfall, ET$_0$ and air temperature (Figure 2). The input [SOURCE: Page_268]

335   variables are spatially distributed. The simulated variables per spatial unit type are shown in Figure 2. The [SOURCE: Page_268]

336   parameters adopted in the equations and relations implemented in the simulators are listed in Appendix C. They [SOURCE: Page_268]

337   correspond to either empirical values or functional properties of the spatial units. They can be either global (i.e., a [SOURCE: Page_268]

338   unique and common value for all the spatial unit types) or spatially distributed (i.e., each spatial unit has its own [SOURCE: Page_268]

339   value). The initial model conditions include the soil water content in all agricultural and non-agricultural SUs, the [SOURCE: Page_268]

340   water level in each GU, and the volume of water stored in each RE, connected or not. [SOURCE: Page_268]

341   2. Materials and methods [SOURCE: Page_269]

342   2.1 Study area [SOURCE: Page_269]

343   The Gélon catchment was chosen for the application of the model, for the hydrologic year 2014-2015, for which [SOURCE: Page_269]

344   most of the data required for model implementation and evaluation was available, notably the agricultural plot [SOURCE: Page_269]

345   map. [SOURCE: Page_269]

346   2.1.1 General characteristics [SOURCE: Page_269]

347   The Gélon is a 19.8-km² catchment belonging to the Arrats catchment, which is a 620 km² sub-catchment of the [SOURCE: Page_269]

348   Garonne River located in southwestern France in the Gers department (Figure 3). The outlet is located at [SOURCE: Page_269]

349   43°51'38"N-0°48'07"E. It is a hilly catchment with the elevation ranging from 110 to 193 m above sea level. The [SOURCE: Page_269]

350   soils are mainly composed of alluvial and molassic slope deposits (Party et al., 2016). The lithology is globally [SOURCE: Page_269]

351   impermeable, without a deep aquifer, which leads to a high density of the hydrographic network (Cavaillé and [SOURCE: Page_269]

352   BRGM, 1968). The total length of the Gélon stream is 8 km. The oceanic climate of the catchment induces a [SOURCE: Page_269]

353   rainfall of 675 mm, an ET$_0$ level of 905 mm and a temperature of 13.5°C on average over the period from 1989- [SOURCE: Page_269]

354   2016. [SOURCE: Page_269]

355 [SOURCE: Page_269]

356 [SOURCE: Page_269]

43   17 [SOURCE: Page_269]

44                                                                                                                     18 [SOURCE: Page_270]

357    Figure 3: Location and map of the Gélon catchment. The agricultural and non-agricultural plots in the map are [SOURCE: Page_270]

358     marked in green and yellow, respectively. The outlet is indicated by a red dot. The hydrographic network and [SOURCE: Page_270]

359                    small reservoirs are represented by blue lines and dark blue areas, respectively. [SOURCE: Page_270]

360   The Gélon catchment is mostly agricultural. The majority (75%) of the catchment area is devoted to agriculture, [SOURCE: Page_270]

361   representing 585 cultivated plots (IGN, 2015). The remaining 25% (244 plots) comprises non-cultivated, [SOURCE: Page_270]

362   urbanized or forested areas (MTES, 2012). The whole cultivated area is covered by annual field crops, and the [SOURCE: Page_270]

363   main crops are straw cereals (mostly wheat, barley, triticale and oats) and sunflower (accounting for 41 % and [SOURCE: Page_270]

364   33 %, respectively, of the cultivated area in 2015). Maize, soybeans, peas, chickpeas, lentils, flax, market [SOURCE: Page_270]

365   gardening (largely garlic, strawberry, butternut and onion), sorghum, rapeseed, and temporary and permanent [SOURCE: Page_270]

366   grassland are also cultivated to a lesser extent in this region where organic farming is increasingly applied. [SOURCE: Page_270]

367   Most crops are rainfed (sunflower, permanent grassland and vineyard plots), some are systematically irrigated [SOURCE: Page_270]

368   (mostly maize and soybeans), and others are irrigated only when weather conditions are particularly dry (straw [SOURCE: Page_270]

369   cereals, temporary grassland, market gardening, rapeseed and orchards). Field surveys indicate that farmers [SOURCE: Page_270]

370   generally irrigate their fields with an amount of 30 mm, except for rapeseed, which can be irrigated only once, at [SOURCE: Page_270]

371   the sowing time, with half the amount (i.e., 15 mm). Irrigation occurs during the cropping season, namely, [SOURCE: Page_270]

372   temporary grasslands are irrigated from April to mid-May, straw cereals from mid-May to mid-June, maize from [SOURCE: Page_270]

373   mid-May to mid-September, market gardening from mid-May to mid-October, soybeans and orchards from June [SOURCE: Page_270]

374   to September, and rapeseed in September. [SOURCE: Page_270]

375   The catchment contains 25 water reservoirs of varying capacities (100 to 30,000 m^3), 13 of which are used for [SOURCE: Page_270]

376   irrigation, while the remaining 12 reservoirs, often smaller, have no current irrigation use following the change to [SOURCE: Page_270]

377   non-irrigated crops or following the purchase of the land by private individuals who are not farmers. The 13 [SOURCE: Page_270]

378   reservoirs are the only resource for irrigation water, i.e., in this catchment, no water is withdrawn from the river. [SOURCE: Page_270]

379   There are no channel networks: the water is directly pumped from the reservoirs and distributed to the fields [SOURCE: Page_270]

380   under pressure. Overall, 19 % of the agricultural area is irrigated, mainly by aspersion using 25-m travelling guns. [SOURCE: Page_270]

381   The limited availability of irrigation equipment, the time required to install the equipment and the limited flow rate [SOURCE: Page_270]

382   of the equipment result in a delay between two irrigations of 6 or 7 days depending on the crop. [SOURCE: Page_270]

383   2.1.2 Weather, pedological, agricultural and hydrological data [SOURCE: Page_271]

384   The weather variables were retrieved from the SAFRAN database of MeteoFrance (Durand et al., 1993), namely, [SOURCE: Page_271]

385   the hourly rainfall and air temperature and daily ET$_0$ calculated according to Penman’s formula, at an 8 km x 8 [SOURCE: Page_271]

386   km resolution. The map of the agricultural plots includes the land use at the field plot level and is available on a [SOURCE: Page_271]

387   yearly basis from the French Land Parcel Identification System (IGN, 2015). Crop yield data are only available at [SOURCE: Page_271]

388   the Gers department level (6,200 km²) from data collected from agricultural cooperatives by public authorities [SOURCE: Page_271]

389   (DRAAF Occitanie, 2020). No database provides information about the agricultural practices in the Gélon [SOURCE: Page_271]

390   catchment, but specific surveys offer insights on the irrigation practices in the Gélon and Arrats catchments. [SOURCE: Page_271]

391   The soil data were provided by the Référentiel Régional Pédologique, a French soil database (Party et al., [SOURCE: Page_271]

392   2016). [SOURCE: Page_271]

393   Stream discharge data at the Gélon outlet have only been available since 14/09/2018. We thus estimated the [SOURCE: Page_271]

394   2014-2015 discharge from the daily specific stream runoff data recorded at the closest station of the French [SOURCE: Page_271]

395   station hydrometric network, assuming that both specific stream runoffs were equal. This assumption was [SOURCE: Page_271]

396   carefully verified over the period 14/09/2018 to 13/09/2019 at a daily time step during which the discharge at both [SOURCE: Page_271]

397   catchment outlets was monitored. The similarity was very high for 47% of stream runoff (i.e., between 0.086 and [SOURCE: Page_271]

398   1.0 mm/d) encountered in the Gélon catchment, with an r² value of 0.68 considering linear regression, an NSEQ [SOURCE: Page_271]

399   value of 0.53 and an NSEsqrt value of 0.71 (Figure 4). The similarity was low for extreme stream runoff, lower than [SOURCE: Page_271]

400   0.086 mm/d (an r² value of 0.02) or higher than 1.0 mm/d (an r² value of 0.11). [SOURCE: Page_271]

403   2.2 Model implementation [SOURCE: Page_272]

404   2.2.1 Spatial segmentation [SOURCE: Page_272]

405   Several geographic data sources (Table 2) were adopted to determine and characterise the geometrical [SOURCE: Page_272]

406   properties of all spatial units of the Gélon catchment, resulting in 25 REs, 17 GUs, 365 RSs and 2402 SUs, 1666 [SOURCE: Page_272]

407   of which are agricultural SUs. [SOURCE: Page_272]

409   2.2.2 Parametrisation [SOURCE: Page_273]

410   As far as possible, the parameters corresponding to the functional properties (Appendix C) were determined from [SOURCE: Page_273]

411   existing databases, measurements and in situ observations or retrieved from the literature. [SOURCE: Page_273]

412   Values of crop growth parameters were fixed based on previous studies. Indeed, these parameters were [SOURCE: Page_273]

413   determined previously for several field crops in southwestern France and then validated for three rainfed and [SOURCE: Page_273]

414   irrigated spring crops (sunflower, maize, and sorghum) (Constantin et al., 2015), for wheat on 14 experimental [SOURCE: Page_273]

415   sites in France and for rotations on two sites in southwestern France (Tribouillois et al., 2018). We grouped crops [SOURCE: Page_273]

416   into classes to limit the number of crop parameter sets, especially for minority crops. For example, the soybean [SOURCE: Page_273]

417   class includes soybeans as the main crop but also peas, chickpeas, flax and lentils as minority crops. The soil [SOURCE: Page_273]

418   texture and soil depth also used in the crop growth model are parameters derived from the French soil database [SOURCE: Page_273]

419   (Référentiel Régional Pédologique, Party et al., 2016) by considering the dominant soil type in each SU. The soils [SOURCE: Page_273]

420   of the agricultural SU show low variability (all clay-loam soils) and all belong to a single soil class. In addition, the [SOURCE: Page_273]

421   three shape parameters of the SU infiltration capacity curve (Equation 1) not defined in the AqYield database, [SOURCE: Page_273]

422   namely, Imax, Ks and 𝜆, were adjusted as detailed below. Two of the four parameters of the GU storage-discharge [SOURCE: Page_273]

423   function were defined based on an analysis of Gélon outflow discharges during recession periods, while the other [SOURCE: Page_273]

424   two, namely, parameters a and b of Equation 2, were fitted. A simple calibration of the outflow at the outlet of the [SOURCE: Page_273]

425   Gélon was performed by considering 3 values for each of the 5 parameters to be fitted and by varying them one [SOURCE: Page_273]

426   at a time. Thus, only 243 sets of parameters were then tested. The three values were chosen to explore a [SOURCE: Page_273]

427   realistic range of variation by selecting the minimum and maximum values found in the literature and their [SOURCE: Page_273]

428   arithmetic mean. The extreme values for the parameters of the SU infiltration curve were defined according to [SOURCE: Page_273]

429   Mishra et al. (2003), Fernández-Pato et al. (2016), Party et al. (2016) and those for the GU storage-discharge [SOURCE: Page_273]

430   function from Kirchner (2009). [SOURCE: Page_273]

432   2.2.3 Time step of the simulation [SOURCE: Page_274]

433   An hourly simulation time step was adopted for all the hydrological processes (blue boxes, Figure 2), except for [SOURCE: Page_274]

434   those processes for which the formalism required a daily time step, as indicated in Section 1, namely, the water [SOURCE: Page_274]

435   balance of agricultural plots as well as crop growth processes, and crop and agricultural water management [SOURCE: Page_274]

436   operations (red and green boxes, Figure 2). [SOURCE: Page_274]

437   2.2.4 Climate input variables and initial conditions [SOURCE: Page_274]

438   Climate input variables, namely, rainfall, ET$_0$ and air temperature were considered spatially uniform in the [SOURCE: Page_274]

439   application of the model to the Gélon catchment. Due to the lack of data, all the initial conditions were set using a [SOURCE: Page_274]

440   warm-up approach, consisting of a simulation over a period long enough to reach equilibrium (Kollet and Maxwell, [SOURCE: Page_274]

441   2008). In this study, we adopted the recursive simulation approach described by Ajami et al. (2014): the previous [SOURCE: Page_274]

442   hydrological year from 2013-2014 was repeated 25 times with constant crop rotations. We verified that the [SOURCE: Page_274]

443   equilibrium state was reached after these 25 year-long simulations by determining whether the annual simulated [SOURCE: Page_274]

444   variations in water storage at a one-year interval were lower than 1% in 95% of the units of each type. This warm- [SOURCE: Page_274]

445   up process was initiated considering a full saturation of the catchment, including a complete filling of the [SOURCE: Page_274]

446   reservoirs to limit the spin-up time (Rahman et al., 2016). [SOURCE: Page_274]

447   2.3 Model verification [SOURCE: Page_274]

448   To verify the model, we considered virtual and real catchments and monitored i) each simulator, ii) the model [SOURCE: Page_274]

449   determinism and iii) the conservation of water volumes. Furthermore, the computation time was also analysed. [SOURCE: Page_274]

450   2.3.1 Simulator testing [SOURCE: Page_274]

451   For each simulator, the agreement between the computer code and conceptual model was verified using simple [SOURCE: Page_274]

452   test cases. The verifications were based on a comparison of the simulated and expected values of the variables, [SOURCE: Page_274]

453   with the latter obtained from either algebraic equations or reference simulations. These tests also allowed us to [SOURCE: Page_274]

454   evaluate the hydrological and agronomic links between all the units. [SOURCE: Page_274]

455   As an example, the combined testing of the irrigation decision and application simulators (Appendix C) allowed us [SOURCE: Page_274]

456   to simultaneously verify the following: [SOURCE: Page_274]

53   22 [SOURCE: Page_274]

54                                                                                                                  23 [SOURCE: Page_275]

457        ●   the identification of all the RE or RS dedicated to irrigation and the links between that water resource [SOURCE: Page_275]

458            and the irrigable SUs, [SOURCE: Page_275]

459        ●   the consistency between the available water volume, water withdrawal volume, irrigation water demand [SOURCE: Page_275]

460            and irrigation amount provided to crops, and [SOURCE: Page_275]

461        ●   the absence of withdrawal from a water resource not dedicated to irrigation. [SOURCE: Page_275]

462   2.3.2 Model determinism [SOURCE: Page_275]

463   Model determinism is guaranteed when identical simulations, repeated in the same computing environment with [SOURCE: Page_275]

464   unchanged parameterizations, initial conditions and boundary conditions, result in exactly the same simulated [SOURCE: Page_275]

465   values. A numerical test was performed on a sub-catchment of the Gélon catchment, modelled with 341 SUs, 112 [SOURCE: Page_275]

466   RSs, 69 GUs and 13 REs, with one of the latter being dedicated to irrigation. The test was executed by repeating [SOURCE: Page_275]

467   the same 5-year simulation 1,000 times, and we assessed whether the water volumes in the GUs, REs, and SUs [SOURCE: Page_275]

468   and water fluxes in the SUs and RSs remained unchanged across the whole catchment. [SOURCE: Page_275]

469   2.3.3 Water volume conservation [SOURCE: Page_275]

470   Water volume conservation is an important criterion in hydrological model verification. We monitored the water [SOURCE: Page_275]

471   volume conservation in MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs at the daily resolution considering the whole catchment. In [SOURCE: Page_275]

472   the case of perfect water volume conservation, the total volume of all simulated outflows from the catchment [SOURCE: Page_275]

473   equals the total volume corresponding to the variation in the simulated water storage and all simulated inflows to [SOURCE: Page_275]

474   the catchment. We monitored the water mass conservation level in the same real catchment as was adopted for [SOURCE: Page_275]

475   model determinism assessment (section 2.3.2, Model determinism) at the daily time step, considering that the [SOURCE: Page_275]

476   difference between the above two volumes should remain below 0.001% of the total inflow volume. [SOURCE: Page_275]

477   2.4 Model evaluation [SOURCE: Page_275]

478   Model evaluation determines the ability to simulate hydrological and agricultural functioning in a real case study. [SOURCE: Page_275]

479   Basically, the evaluation relies on the comparison of simulated variables to available observed, or reference, [SOURCE: Page_275]

480   data. As the primary intention in using MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs is to quantify the cumulative effects of [SOURCE: Page_275]

481   reservoirs on crop yields and on stream runoff at the catchment outlet, we chose these two variables to evaluate [SOURCE: Page_275]

55   23 [SOURCE: Page_275]

56                                                                                                                   24 [SOURCE: Page_276]

482   the model. The evaluation therefore followed two steps. The first step involved the evaluation of the model in the [SOURCE: Page_276]

483   simulation of global variables corresponding to the annual fluxes across the entire catchment for which reference [SOURCE: Page_276]

484   data were available for the case study. In the second step, the model ability to finely simulate the daily stream [SOURCE: Page_276]

485   runoff was analysed using the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (1970) calculated as follows: [SOURCE: Page_276]

486 [SOURCE: Page_276]

487 [SOURCE: Page_276]

488   where NSEq is the Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency of the stream runoff, qoi is the reference stream runoff at the ith time [SOURCE: Page_276]

489   index, q o is the mean reference stream runoff and qsi is the simulated stream runoff at the ith time index. The [SOURCE: Page_276]

490   closer the value is to 1, the higher the quality of the stream runoff simulation is. The efficiency considering the [SOURCE: Page_276]

491   square root of the stream runoff, denoted as NSEsqrt, was also calculated since it assigns a high weight to low [SOURCE: Page_276]

492   values of the stream runoff when NSEq is highly sensitive to high flows (Oudin et al., 2006; Pushpalatha et al., [SOURCE: Page_276]

493   2012). [SOURCE: Page_276]

494   When applying the model to the Gélon catchment, the efficiencies were calculated based on the daily stream [SOURCE: Page_276]

495   runoff over the full hydrologic year of 2014/2015 starting on 1 September. The daily simulated stream runoff, qsi, [SOURCE: Page_276]

496   was calculated as the sum of hourly simulated stream runoff for the ith day. As we determined that the stream [SOURCE: Page_276]

497   runoff data used as reference data were less reliable between June and October and for stream runoff below the [SOURCE: Page_276]

498   threshold of 0.086 mm/d (cf section 2.1.2), we also calculated the efficiencies by considering those days when the [SOURCE: Page_276]

499   stream runoff exceeded the above threshold, excluding the period from June to October. [SOURCE: Page_276]

500   2.5 Numerical explorations [SOURCE: Page_276]

501   The model was then applied to simulate, in the Gélon catchment, two situations that differed in terms of crop [SOURCE: Page_276]

502   allocation and reservoir water management (Table 3). The objective was to analyse the capacity of the model to [SOURCE: Page_276]

503   predict possible future conditions and assess the potential consequences of different policies in crop and [SOURCE: Page_276]

504   agricultural water management strategies, as is commonly achieved in scenario exercises using models in water [SOURCE: Page_276]

505   resource management (Leenhardt et al., 2012). The “Reference” situation represents the current state, as [SOURCE: Page_276]

508   assumed that all reservoirs of the catchment were used for irrigation purposes and that all agricultural SUs within [SOURCE: Page_277]

516   3. Results [SOURCE: Page_278]

517   3.1 Model verification [SOURCE: Page_278]

518   3.1.1 Simulator testing, model determinism and water volume conservation [SOURCE: Page_278]

519   Testing of all the simulators was successful since the variables simulated with the model matched the expected [SOURCE: Page_278]

520   values. The results are not presented but are available upon request. The model determinism was verified since [SOURCE: Page_278]

521   the simulated variables in terms of the total water storage in the GUs, SUs and REs and water fluxes (surface [SOURCE: Page_278]

522   runoff in the SUs and stream runoff in the RSs) were strictly identical for all 1,000 simulations. Water volume [SOURCE: Page_278]

523   conservation in the simulations was also verified: at the annual scale, the error was lower than 0.0001 % of the [SOURCE: Page_278]

524   inflow volume. [SOURCE: Page_278]

525   3.1.2 Computation time [SOURCE: Page_278]

526   The simulation was performed based on an Ubuntu Quad-Core microprocessor at 2.90 GHz, with 128 GB of [SOURCE: Page_278]

527   RAM and a 32-bit CPU. The computation time reached 17 hours for a 26-year period in the Gélon catchment, [SOURCE: Page_278]

528   with a display of the daily global variables in the whole domain and an additional display of all of the variables in [SOURCE: Page_278]

529   each spatial unit (3 per RS and GU, 7 per RE and 30 per SU) for the last simulated year, which represents 4.7 [SOURCE: Page_278]

530   Go. [SOURCE: Page_278]

531   3.2 Model evaluation [SOURCE: Page_278]

532   At the catchment level, the simulated stream runoff over the hydrological year of 2014/2015 is 102.8 mm (Table [SOURCE: Page_278]

533   4), which is only 6.4% higher than the reference stream runoff (96.6 mm). The efficiencies of NSEq and NSEsqrtq of [SOURCE: Page_278]

534   the simulated daily stream runoff are 0.32 and 0.26, respectively. In regard to the days when the stream runoff [SOURCE: Page_278]

535   exceeds 0.086 mm/d between November and May, when the reference stream data are considered reliable [SOURCE: Page_278]

536   (please refer to section 2.4), the calculated NSEq and NSEsqrtq values are both 0.47. These values approaching [SOURCE: Page_278]

537   0.5 indicate that the model yields nearly satisfactory results not only for high flows, in terms of NSEq (Moriasi et [SOURCE: Page_278]

538   al., 2015), but also for low flows, in terms of NSEsqrtq (Oudin et al., 2006). Over the period corresponding to these [SOURCE: Page_278]

541   runoff (80.0 mm). According to Moriasi et al. (2015), an error of less than 5% is considered very good. On the [SOURCE: Page_279]

583   3.3.2 Spatially distributed variables [SOURCE: Page_283]

584   MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs simulates a large number of spatially distributed variables related to the hydrological [SOURCE: Page_283]

585   and agricultural responses of a catchment. We illustrate three of them, namely, i) stream runoff, ii) irrigation water [SOURCE: Page_283]

586   demand and iii) reservoir filling rate evolution. [SOURCE: Page_283]

587   The stream runoff is simulated along the whole hydrographic network at the RS resolution. This allows us to [SOURCE: Page_283]

588   assess and compare the inner-catchment variability, as shown in Figure 7, where the difference in the monthly [SOURCE: Page_283]

589   stream runoff along the hydrographic network between the Reference and All-RE situations in December 2014 [SOURCE: Page_283]

590   and July 2015 is plotted. These two months were chosen because they corresponded to high flow and low flow [SOURCE: Page_283]

591   periods, respectively. In that respect, several results can be highlighted. The first result is that the relative [SOURCE: Page_283]

592   variation in the monthly stream runoff between the situations at the catchment outlet differs from one month to [SOURCE: Page_283]

71   31 [SOURCE: Page_283]

72                                                                                                                    32 [SOURCE: Page_284]

593   another and that the variation in the annual stream runoff also differs. For example, although the simulated [SOURCE: Page_284]

594   annual runoff in the All-RE situation was lower by -6% compared to the Reference situation, the difference of [SOURCE: Page_284]

595   monthly stream runoff between both situations was -3% in July and -14% in December. The second notable result [SOURCE: Page_284]

596   is that the variation in the stream runoff at the outlet may mask the high variability in stream runoff along the [SOURCE: Page_284]

597   hydrographic network. The simulated stream runoff variation was negative in most of the stream reaches (Figure [SOURCE: Page_284]

598   7), indicating a lower stream runoff in the All-RE situation than in the Reference situation over the two months [SOURCE: Page_284]

599   analysed. This result was expected due to i) the higher crop water requirement of maize compared to the straw [SOURCE: Page_284]

600   cereals, which is the main irrigated crop in the Reference situation, and ii) the larger water withdrawals in the [SOURCE: Page_284]

601   reservoirs in order to irrigate maize. This leads to emptier reservoirs at the beginning of the rainy period and thus [SOURCE: Page_284]

602   to an increase of water interception of runoff and stream runoff by the reservoirs and to a decrease of the stream [SOURCE: Page_284]

603   runoff in the catchment. However, in July, in the western branch of the hydrographic network, delimited by A and [SOURCE: Page_284]

604   B in Figure 7, the stream runoff was higher (+9%) than that in the Reference situation. This counterintuitive result [SOURCE: Page_284]

605   is explained by an increase of the baseflow in the All-RE situation, which is 8% higher in July for certain GUs in [SOURCE: Page_284]

606   the southwest of the catchment. This increase in the baseflow is first related to the irrigation. Indeed, the absence [SOURCE: Page_284]

607   of irrigation under the Reference situation in the northwest of the catchment (Figure 7) leads to a lower soil water [SOURCE: Page_284]

608   content than that in the All-RE situation, where the soils are cropped with highly irrigated maize. The rainfall in [SOURCE: Page_284]

609   July and the subsequent infiltration allows the soil water content to exceed the soil field capacity faster, thus [SOURCE: Page_284]

610   triggering larger soil percolation in the All-RE situation than in the Reference. However, this phenomenon is [SOURCE: Page_284]

611   limited to a small part of the catchment. Indeed, in the rest of the catchment, the water amount available for [SOURCE: Page_284]

612   irrigation in the reservoirs is smaller than the demand, and the mean soil water content in the All-RE situation [SOURCE: Page_284]

613   remains lower than that in the Reference situation. Thus, at the catchment scale, the stream runoff is slightly [SOURCE: Page_284]

614   modified by these changes and driven more by the increasing AET due to the maize crops. [SOURCE: Page_284]

615   The irrigation water demand also exhibits inner spatial and temporal variability, as shown in Figure 7, where the [SOURCE: Page_284]

616   irrigation water demand is plotted for the Reference and All-RE situations and two months corresponding to the [SOURCE: Page_284]

617   beginning (June) and the end (August) of the irrigation period. These two months illustrate well how the water [SOURCE: Page_284]

618   demand depends on crop requirements and water resource availability in reservoirs, which usually decreases [SOURCE: Page_284]

73   32 [SOURCE: Page_284]

74                                                                                                                      33 [SOURCE: Page_285]

619   with time during the irrigation period . The water demand is quite uniform in the catchment for the All-RE situation [SOURCE: Page_285]

620   because all irrigated fields are cropped with the same crop, maize. The difference in water demand between June [SOURCE: Page_285]

621   and August relies mainly on this situation in crop water requirements. In June, the maize was planted a few [SOURCE: Page_285]

622   weeks earlier, and the crop water requirement, and thus the water demand for irrigation, is low. In August, the [SOURCE: Page_285]

623   crop requirement is large due to the crop development and the high ET$_0$ (Figure 5). As the reservoirs are empty [SOURCE: Page_285]

624   at this time (Figure 8), the water demand remains high most of the time. In the reference situation, water demand [SOURCE: Page_285]

625   is slightly more variable than for the All-RE situation because there are different irrigated crops, such as straw [SOURCE: Page_285]

626   cereals, soybean and maize. The crop development in time and the irrigation period are different from one crop to [SOURCE: Page_285]

627   another one. As straw cereals are harvested in July, all fields with this crop are simulated with a zero water [SOURCE: Page_285]

628   demand in August for the reference situation (fields with black dots in the left map of Figure 7). As in the All-RE [SOURCE: Page_285]

629   situation, the temporal variation in water demand for maize fields between June and August also results from the [SOURCE: Page_285]

630   water availability in the reservoirs. For instance, the simulated water demand for the field in maize indicated by a [SOURCE: Page_285]

631   red circle in Figure 7 varies from zero in June to more than 60 mm in August. The water volume in the reservoir [SOURCE: Page_285]

632   connected to this field (grey line in Figure 8) is not large enough in August to meet the crop requirement, leading [SOURCE: Page_285]

633   to a permanent high water demand. [SOURCE: Page_285]

634   The reservoir filling rate, which is the ratio between the volume of water stored and the RE capacity, also reveals [SOURCE: Page_285]

635   a high spatial and temporal variability (Figure 8). This finding is explained by the spatial distribution of the crops, [SOURCE: Page_285]

636   the different water requirements and cycles of the different crops, and the locations and properties of the [SOURCE: Page_285]

637   reservoirs. Whether a reservoir is used for irrigation or not is the first variation factor of the filling rate between [SOURCE: Page_285]

638   reservoirs: either connected or non-connected, REs remain almost full throughout the year as long as they are [SOURCE: Page_285]

639   not applied for irrigation purposes (the blue and red curves in Figure 8b). The type of irrigated crop is the second [SOURCE: Page_285]

640   factor, namely, in the Reference situation, where the various crops are irrigated, the reservoir levels decrease first [SOURCE: Page_285]

641   in June to irrigate the straw cereal, market gardening and soybean crops and again from July to September when [SOURCE: Page_285]

642   the maize and soybean crops are irrigated (the orange, green, grey and black lines in Figure 8b), while in the All- [SOURCE: Page_285]

643   RE situation with all irrigated plots cropped with maize, the decrease in June is not observed (all the coloured [SOURCE: Page_285]

644   lines in Figure 8c). The type of reservoir, connected or non-connected, is another factor explaining the differences [SOURCE: Page_285]

75   33 [SOURCE: Page_285]

76                                                                                                                       34 [SOURCE: Page_286]

645   in filling rate. When the irrigation water demand is high, as that during maize irrigation in the All-RE situation, the [SOURCE: Page_286]

646   connected reservoirs (the red and orange lines in Figure 8b and 8c) are more likely to become filled because they [SOURCE: Page_286]

647   benefit from both surface and stream runoff from the upstream reach, while the non-connected reservoirs, only [SOURCE: Page_286]

648   receiving surface runoff, are less likely to become filled (the blue and green lines in Figure 8b and 8c). The last [SOURCE: Page_286]

649   factor is the location of the reservoir, as illustrated by the difference between two non-connected reservoirs [SOURCE: Page_286]

650   reserved for irrigation (the black and grey lines, respectively, in Figure 8). In one case (the black line), the drained [SOURCE: Page_286]

651   area is not large enough to fill the reservoir during the surface runoff period, and the reservoir remains almost [SOURCE: Page_286]

652   empty throughout the year regardless of the situation. In the second case (the grey line), the drained area is large [SOURCE: Page_286]

653   enough to support a high filling rate, as indicated by the filling rate approaching the reservoir capacity during the [SOURCE: Page_286]

654   rainfall events in late June. [SOURCE: Page_286]

675   4. Discussion [SOURCE: Page_290]

676   The first application of the MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs model to the Gelon catchment gave promising results [SOURCE: Page_290]

677   (Figure 5; Tables 4 and 5). The main processes underlying the hydrological and agricultural functioning of the [SOURCE: Page_290]

678   catchment seem to be well modelled. However, considering the application of the model to other catchments and [SOURCE: Page_290]

679   other agropedoclimatic contexts requires questioning (i) the availability of the data needed for its application to [SOURCE: Page_290]

680   other real case studies and (ii) the improvements to the model in terms of the processes represented. The two [SOURCE: Page_290]

681   points are discussed hereafter. [SOURCE: Page_290]

682   The first point of discussion concerns the data needed to use the MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs model, either to [SOURCE: Page_290]

683   define forcing variables to obtain the spatial representation of the flow domain to parameterise it on the study [SOURCE: Page_290]

684   area or to evaluate it. Most of the necessary data (e.g., topography, hydrographic network, soil characteristics, [SOURCE: Page_290]

685   nature of crops, and meteorological variables) may be extracted or derived from generic databases, often [SOURCE: Page_290]

686   available throughout Europe. Moreover, as this model is built on already proven models and on widely used [SOURCE: Page_290]

687   equations, some parameters can be fixed from the literature. For example, this is the case for the plant growing [SOURCE: Page_290]

688   coefficients or for the k factor for converting reference evapotranspiration to reservoir evaporation. This makes it [SOURCE: Page_290]

689   easy to envision the use of the model in catchment areas other than the one we studied. [SOURCE: Page_290]

690   However, there is no generic database for all model inputs or for all variables used for its evaluation. In such [SOURCE: Page_290]

691   cases and when available, those data may be derived from local databases, specific surveys or local expertise. [SOURCE: Page_290]

692   This is particularly the case for data on reservoirs: there is currently no database at the European or even the [SOURCE: Page_290]

693   French level that allows a complete and high-quality description of small water reservoirs. The availability and [SOURCE: Page_290]

694   estimation of the small reservoirs properties and the water use from the reservoirs have remained a real [SOURCE: Page_290]

85   38 [SOURCE: Page_290]

86                                                                                                                    39 [SOURCE: Page_291]

695   challenge regardless of the approaches used in catchment hydrological modelling with reservoirs (Hughes and [SOURCE: Page_291]

696   Mantel, 2010, Lowe et al. 2005). This has motivated the development of remote sensing methods to estimate [SOURCE: Page_291]

697   position and capacity of small reservoirs over large areas (Ogilvie et al., 2016). In France, the collective water [SOURCE: Page_291]

698   management structures recently set up in deficit areas ("Organismes Uniques de Gestion Collective de l'Eau") [SOURCE: Page_291]

699   are beginning to create a type of database gathering characteristics and water uses of small reservoirs. [SOURCE: Page_291]

700   Databases describing agricultural practices are also incomplete, either in terms of geographical location or in [SOURCE: Page_291]

701   terms of content, as explained in Leenhardt et al. (2010, 2020). Therefore, this requires the implementation of [SOURCE: Page_291]

702   specific acquisition methods, for example, as presented for cropping systems by Murgue et al. (2016) and Rizzo [SOURCE: Page_291]

703   et al. (2019). It is clear that the lack of generic databases for some of the necessary variables to use or evaluate [SOURCE: Page_291]

704   the model makes using the model more difficult. However, this constraint is not specific to MHYDAS-Small- [SOURCE: Page_291]

705   Reservoirs and has been encountered by other modelling approaches dealing with the cumulative effect of small [SOURCE: Page_291]

706   reservoirs. [SOURCE: Page_291]

707   The quality of the data used also guarantees the predictive quality of the model and the reliability of the model [SOURCE: Page_291]

708   assessment. The use of indirect acquisition methods necessarily introduces inaccuracies, either because of the [SOURCE: Page_291]

709   quality of the expertise (Rizzo et al., 2019) or because of the method itself. For example, in our case study, we [SOURCE: Page_291]

710   did not manage to meet all the owners of the reservoirs (absences or refusals) so that the data for some [SOURCE: Page_291]

711   reservoirs correspond to hypotheses based on our observations or on the expertise of neighbours. However, the [SOURCE: Page_291]

712   existence of generic databases does not exclude the need to examine the quality of the data included in them. [SOURCE: Page_291]

713   For example, in the present study, although we had databases providing stream flow, meteorological data and [SOURCE: Page_291]

714   crop yield values, we were only able to access stream flow data at a nearby station located within the same basin [SOURCE: Page_291]

715   but outside the Gélon catchment, while meteorological data and crop yield values, respectively, were at a [SOURCE: Page_291]

716   resolution that was too low to obtain internal spatial variability on an 8 km² grid and averaged over the entire Gers [SOURCE: Page_291]

717   department,. These spatial discrepancies necessarily affect the quality of the data. More intensive field work, for [SOURCE: Page_291]

718   example, by monitoring flows at the Gélon outlet or by obtaining yield values from agricultural cooperatives or [SOURCE: Page_291]

719   traders who collect crops in this sector, would have enabled a better evaluation of the model's performance. [SOURCE: Page_291]

87   39 [SOURCE: Page_291]

88                                                                                                                    40 [SOURCE: Page_292]

720   The second point of discussion is about the way to improve the modelling of processes in MHYDAS-Small- [SOURCE: Page_292]

721   Reservoirs, in particular processes directly affecting the reservoir. Regarding this point, the modular design of the [SOURCE: Page_292]

722   MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs model under the OpenFLUID platform easily allows adding or improving simulators. [SOURCE: Page_292]

723   In the current version of the model, some processes are neglected. This is the case for infiltration of water from [SOURCE: Page_292]

724   the reservoirs to the underlying groundwater or conversely for the discharge of groundwater directly to the [SOURCE: Page_292]

725   reservoirs. Neglecting these processes appeared to be acceptable in the Gélon catchment given the [SOURCE: Page_292]

726   characteristics of the reservoirs and their connection to the groundwater. However, depending on the pedological [SOURCE: Page_292]

727   and lithological contexts and the properties of the reservoirs, in particular the hydrodynamic properties of the [SOURCE: Page_292]

728   reservoir bed, exchanges between the reservoir and the groundwater can be dominant processes in the [SOURCE: Page_292]

729   hydrological dynamics of the reservoir (Bouteffeha et al., 2015). Modelling the exchanges would therefore [SOURCE: Page_292]

730   improve the model in its ability to simulate a diversity of contexts. The modelling could be done simply by [SOURCE: Page_292]

731   considering the differences in water levels between the reservoir and groundwater. This type of relationship is [SOURCE: Page_292]

732   reported to well predict the dynamics of exchanges in various contexts (Sharda et al., 2006). [SOURCE: Page_292]

733   Another improvement of the model is in the modelling of the water management rules of the reservoirs. Indeed, [SOURCE: Page_292]

734   the cumulative hydrological effect of reservoir networks cannot be explained solely by the geometric [SOURCE: Page_292]

735   characteristics of the network (density in terms of number of reservoirs, volume or surface area). The [SOURCE: Page_292]

736   management rules of the reservoirs, which sometimes differ from one reservoir to another, appear to be an [SOURCE: Page_292]

737   important factor in this effect (Habets et al., 2018; Hughes and Mantel, 2010). In the present case study, the [SOURCE: Page_292]

738   sharing of available water in a reservoir is modelled by a fairly standard approach by considering that the water [SOURCE: Page_292]

739   withdrawn is distributed to the irrigated field proportionally to the water demand, but other priority rules could be [SOURCE: Page_292]

740   considered. Priority could be given, for example, to crops providing high financial incomes. We could also [SOURCE: Page_292]

741   consider defining rules based on short-term weather predictions. For actual water management rules being [SOURCE: Page_292]

742   modelled within a specific simulator, the modular design of the MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs model will be a clear [SOURCE: Page_292]

743   asset to allow various water management modalities. [SOURCE: Page_292]

744   5. Conclusions [SOURCE: Page_293]

745 [SOURCE: Page_293]

746   The MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs model has been developed to understand and predict the local and cumulative [SOURCE: Page_293]

747   hydrologic and agricultural effects of a reservoir network in an agricultural catchment. Hydrological models are [SOURCE: Page_293]

748   already available to assess the cumulative impact of reservoir networks. Compared to these models, the [SOURCE: Page_293]

749   originality of MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs lies in two of its features. The first is that it integrates processes related [SOURCE: Page_293]

750   to the three major components of the catchment's agro-hydrological functioning: hydrology, crop growth, and [SOURCE: Page_293]

751   water management decisions. The second feature is that it explicitly represents the main elements of the [SOURCE: Page_293]

752   agricultural catchment - the plot, the reach, the reservoir, and the water table - and the hydrological and [SOURCE: Page_293]

753   agricultural relationships between these elements. In addition, the model distinguishes between reservoirs [SOURCE: Page_293]

754   according to their connection to the hydrographic networks. In doing so, it allows the simulation of both local [SOURCE: Page_293]

755   effects in the immediate environment of each reservoir and cumulative effects on overall yields (Table 6) and [SOURCE: Page_293]

756   flows (Figure 6). [SOURCE: Page_293]

757   Numerical verification of the model was successful. The first application of the model to a 19-km² catchment gave [SOURCE: Page_293]

758   promising results in terms of stream runoff and crop yield simulations. However, the evaluation and validation of [SOURCE: Page_293]

759   the model are incomplete. The model could be improved in two directions. The first concerns its validation, with [SOURCE: Page_293]

760   an analysis of the model performance to simulate the variables for which it was intended, such as stream runoff, [SOURCE: Page_293]

761   crop yields and water withdrawals and availability in small reservoirs. Model validation could also gain from its [SOURCE: Page_293]

762   application to catchments where comprehensive, reliable and distributed data sets, such as water tables, stream [SOURCE: Page_293]

763   runoff and crop yield data, are available based on in situ measurements and observations. The second direction [SOURCE: Page_293]

764   would be to perform a sensitivity analysis. In particular, a sensitivity analysis of the reservoir characteristics and of [SOURCE: Page_293]

765   the parameters associated with water dynamics modelling in small reservoirs could be helpful when [SOURCE: Page_293]

766   parameterizing the model in future applications. Thus, the MHYDAS-Small-Reservoirs model could potentially be [SOURCE: Page_293]

767   adopted by land use planners and water managers to assist them in their decisions regarding new small-reservoir [SOURCE: Page_293]

768   projects in catchments or management of the water stored in reservoirs. [SOURCE: Page_293]

1054   Appendix A: Simulation rules used for farmer management decisions [SOURCE: Page_307]

1055   The farmer management decisions considered in the model include tillage, sowing, harvest and irrigation. The [SOURCE: Page_307]

1056   decision rules adopted to simulate these technical operations are described below. The variables employed as [SOURCE: Page_307]

1057   indicators are mentioned between brackets. [SOURCE: Page_307]

1058   ●        A tillage day occurs during the tillage period (temporal window) according to the soil type, when the soil [SOURCE: Page_307]

1059   water content is favourable, i.e., this depends on the weather conditions (antecedent cumulative rainfall) and soil [SOURCE: Page_307]

1060   conditions (soil water content); [SOURCE: Page_307]

1061   ●        A sowing day may occur on the first day of the simulation or after the harvesting period, which depends [SOURCE: Page_307]

1062   on the weather conditions (antecedent cumulative rainfall and minimal temperature), possible sowing period [SOURCE: Page_307]

1063   (temporal window) according to the crop type and precocity class and soil conditions (soil water content); [SOURCE: Page_307]

1064   ●        A harvesting day is simulated either when the crop is mature (crop development stage) or before poor [SOURCE: Page_307]

1065   soil and weather conditions occur (antecedent cumulative rainfall and soil water content), which could result in [SOURCE: Page_307]

1066   soil damage; [SOURCE: Page_307]

1067   ●        Depending on the development of the crop and the weather conditions (previous rainfall and rainfall [SOURCE: Page_307]

1068   forecasts), the water demand for irrigation may be zero or have a non-zero fixed value. This fixed value depends [SOURCE: Page_307]

1069   on the crop, the soil and the irrigation equipment. It is a model parameter (e.g., 30 mm for maize in the Gelon [SOURCE: Page_307]

1070   catchment application). The volume of water actually withdrawn and delivered to the cultivated field is conditioned [SOURCE: Page_307]

1071   by the availability of the water resource (see section 1.4.2). The farmer's water demand is calculated at a time [SOURCE: Page_307]

1072   step depending on the farmer's equipment constraints. The time step is a model parameter (e.g., 6 or 7 days in [SOURCE: Page_307]

1073   the Gelon catchment application depending on the field). [SOURCE: Page_307]
